results.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
results.answer:
Yes.  Because a shop that serves the public is a **public accommodation** under the ADA, you are required to remove “barriers that are readily achievable.”  The ADA specifically says that private businesses that provide goods or services to the public are covered by its public‑accommodation provisions, and that existing facilities must be made accessible when doing so is *readily achievable* (the determination is based on the size and resources of the business).  

- The handbook states that a private business that serves the public is a public accommodation and must remove barriers that are readily achievable:  
  *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)*

- The same section explains that existing facilities are **not exempt** from these requirements and that barriers such as doors, ramps, and other physical features must be made accessible if it can be done with reasonable effort.  
  *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)*

- For a shop, this means at least one entrance must be accessible and an accessible route must be provided to the interior.  If a shop has only one public entrance, that entrance must be made accessible; if it has two entrances, at least one must be accessible.  In addition, the shop must provide accessible routes to goods and services.  
  *[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)*

So, if making your shop wheelchair‑accessible is *readily achievable* for you (e.g., you can install or modify a door, create a ramp, or otherwise remove the barrier without excessive cost or difficulty), you are required to do so to comply with the ADA.



**Sources:**
1. [ada_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 6)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)
2. [ada_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 10)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)

results.question: what do i need to do to keep employees safe and my premises accessible
results.answer:
To keep your workers safe **and** make the premises accessible, the handbook offers two sets of guidance:

**1. Workplace safety (OSHA)**  

| What to do | Where it’s stated | Why it matters |
|------------|-------------------|----------------|
| Develop a written safety‑and‑health program that sets out management leadership, worker participation, hazard identification, hazard control, training, and program evaluation | *Implementing a Safety and Health Program* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7) | The program is the foundation for all other safety actions. |
| Conduct regular self‑inspections to spot hazards, verify controls, and keep records | *Workplace Self‑Inspection* [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8) | Self‑inspections let you keep hazards under control before they cause injury. |
| Put a written emergency action plan in place that defines roles, communications, and medical‑assistance procedures | *Emergency Action Plans* [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=25) | An emergency plan is required when any OSHA standard requires one, and it protects workers when an incident happens. |
| Follow the “General Duty Clause” that obligates every employer to provide a work environment free from recognized hazards that could cause death or serious harm | *General Duty Clause* [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91) | This is the core OSHA requirement; any hazard that isn’t covered by a specific OSHA standard must still be eliminated. |

**2. Premises accessibility (ADA)**  

| What to do | Where it’s stated | Key figures or deadlines |
|------------|-------------------|--------------------------|
| Install an accessible entrance (e.g., ramp, turnstile replacement, or alternate door) that has a slope no steeper than 1:12, handrails whenever the slope is steeper than 1:20 and the vertical rise is > 6 in. | *Accessible Entrance* [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10) | “The slope of the ramp should be … not more than 1:12” and “handrails … when the slope is more that 1:20 and the vertical rise is greater than 6 in.” |
| Add a sign that points to the accessible entrance if another entrance is not accessible; the sign must be ≤ 48 in. high to accommodate users. | *Accessible Entrance* [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10) | “The alternate entrance must be open… If the alternative accessible entrance is not left unlocked … you must provide an accessible way for notifying staff to open the door, such as a buzzer or bell.  The buzzer or call bell must be … at a height generally not more than 48 in above ground.” |
| Provide accessible parking spaces that are at least 8 ft. wide, have an access aisle 5 ft. (cars) or 8 ft. (vans) wide, and are located on level ground close to the accessible entrance. | *Accessible Parking* [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8) | “An accessible parking space must have … an access aisle … 5 ft. wide for cars… 8 ft. wide for vans.” |
| Ensure all sales and service counters are no higher than 36 in. and at least 36 in. long, with a clear floor space 30 in. × 48 in. in front of them. | *Sales and Service Counters* [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) | “Accessible counter is at least 36" long and not more than 36" above the floor… Provide a 30" by 48" space in front of the sales or service counter.” |
| Use accessible door hardware (lever handle or thumb‑latch disabled) instead of round knobs or tight‑grasp knobs. | *Doors at Entrances to Businesses* [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12) | “A round door knob… requires the user to tightly grasp… A lever handle is accessible because it can be operated without tight grasping, pinching or twisting.” |
| Remove or replace narrow turnstiles or security gates with an accessible passage, gate, or a manually operated door. | *Turning Stiles and Security Gates* [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13) | “If an inaccessible turnstile … no accessible gate… it must be replaced or removed or an alternative accessible entrance provided, if doing so is readily achievable.” |

**Putting it all together**

1. Write a safety‑and‑health program (page 7), and perform routine self‑inspections (page 8).  
2. Draft an emergency action plan (page 25) and maintain the General Duty Clause baseline (page 91).  
3. Make the building physically accessible: install a ramp or alternate door (page 10), post directional signage (page 10), add accessible parking (page 8), set up accessible counters (page 15), and fit usable door hardware (page 12).  

Follow each passage exactly as written, and you’ll satisfy both OSHA safety requirements and ADA accessibility mandates.

results.question: what should i track for taxes and for travel expenses
results.answer:
**What you should keep in your books for tax‑related records**

| What to keep | Why it matters | Document­‑source |
|--------------|----------------|-----------------|
| **Receipts, invoices, bills and canceled checks** for every purchase, sale, payroll, rent, loan, insurance, and other deductible expense. These are the primary documents that prove a transaction occurred and how much you paid. | The IRS requires that each deduction on your return be supported by “source documents.” | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13) |
| **Bank statements and deposit slips** that show the money that entered or left your business account. | They confirm the amounts recorded in your books and help you reconcile monthly cash receipts. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12) |
| **Daily summaries of cash receipts and a monthly cash‑receipt book** (if you keep a cash‑based system). | They provide a quick audit trail for all cash inflows during the year. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **Monthly check‑disbursement journals** and a ledger that totals each expense category. | They keep a clean record of each payment and the purpose of every dollar spent. | (irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 15‑17) |
| **Depreciation worksheets** (or the equivalent for any fixed assets you own). | Depreciation is a major deductible expense; the worksheet provides the details the IRS wants for the deduction. | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=17) |
| **Payroll records** (if you have employees): hours worked, wages, wages withheld, employment‑tax payments, and the related W‑2/W‑3 or other wage statements. | Employment taxes are separate from income‑tax deductions, so you must keep these for at least four years. | (irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 13‑16) |
| **A copy of your most recent tax return** (Form 1040, Schedule C, etc.) and the supporting schedules that contain the amounts you claimed for business expenses. | The IRS can request these when reviewing your return. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13) |

If you use a cash‑based (single‑entry) system, a simple journal and ledger with the items above is enough. If you use an accrual‑or double‑entry system, you would also keep a chart of accounts and the journal/ledger entries that are posted from your journals to the ledger. Either way, the documents above give the IRS the evidence it requests.

**What you should keep for travel (business‑trip) expenses**

| Item | Why you need to keep it | Document­‑source |
|------|------------------------|-------------------|
| **Mileage log** (date, purpose, destination, business miles, personal miles). | If you claim the **standard mileage rate** for a car or truck, the IRS wants a log to show the miles were truly business miles. | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35) |
| **Receipts for airfare, train, bus, or car rental**. | These are the actual expense amounts you can deduct. | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Receipts or invoices for taxis, ridesharing, or a commuter bus** between the airport or station and your hotel, or between the hotel and your work location away from home. | They are taxable expense categories  | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Receipts for baggage or freight charges** when you send baggage or display material to a temporary work location. | These are deductible as transportation expenses. | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Receipts for lodging and room‑service** at your hotel when traveling away from home. | Lodging is a deductible expense on a business trip that is overnight or long enough that you need to sleep or rest. | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Receipts for meals** (including a note on the type of meal: business discussion, client meeting, etc.). | The IRS usually allows you to deduct **50 %** of the cost of business meals.  | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Receipts for phone calls (if the expense is listed)** and email or fax charges that are used for business while traveling. | They can be deducted as a travel expense if they are necessary for the trip. | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Receipts for tips** (e.g., for hotel staff or transportation carriers). | Tips you give for business travel services are deductible. | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **A calendar or itineraries** that show the scheduling of your trip and the business reasons for each location visited. | Helps prove the trip is “ordinary and necessary” for your business. | (irs_publication



**Sources:**

5. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 35)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35)
6. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 40)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)

| **Daily summaries of cash receipts and a monthly cash‑receipt book** (if you keep a cash‑based system). | They provide a quick audit trail for all cash inflows during the year. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **Monthly check‑disbursement journals** and a ledger that totals each expense category. | They keep a clean record of each payment and the purpose of every dollar spent. | (irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 15‑17) |
| **Depreciation worksheets** (or the equivalent for any fixed assets you own). | Depreciation is a major deductible expense; the worksheet provides the details the IRS wants for the deduction. | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=17) |
| **Payroll records** (if you have employees): hours worked, wages, wages withheld, employment‑tax payments, and the related W‑2/W‑3 or other wage statements. | Employment taxes are separate from income‑tax deductions, so you must keep these for at least four years. | (irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 13‑16) |
| **A copy of your most recent tax return** (Form 1040, Schedule C, etc.) and the supporting schedules that contain the amounts you claimed for business expenses. | The IRS can request these when reviewing your return. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13) |

If you use a cash‑based (single‑entry) system, a simple journal and ledger with the items above is enough. If you use an accrual‑or double‑entry system, you would also keep a chart of accounts and the journal/ledger entries that are posted from your journals to the ledger. Either way, the documents above give the IRS the evidence it requests.

**What you should keep for travel (business‑trip) expenses**

| Item | Why you need to keep it | Document­‑source |
|------|------------------------|-------------------|
| **Mileage log** (date, purpose, destination, business miles, personal miles). | If you claim the **standard mileage rate** for a car or truck, the IRS wants a log to show the miles were truly business miles. | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35) |
| **Receipts for airfare, train, bus, or car rental**. | These are the actual expense amounts you can deduct. | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Receipts or invoices for taxis, ridesharing, or a commuter bus** between the airport or station and your hotel, or between the hotel and your work location away from home. | They are taxable expense categories  | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Receipts for baggage or freight charges** when you send baggage or display material to a temporary work location. | These are deductible as transportation expenses. | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Receipts for lodging and room‑service** at your hotel when traveling away from home. | Lodging is a deductible expense on a business trip that is overnight or long enough that you need to sleep or rest. | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Receipts for meals** (including a note on the type of meal: business discussion, client meeting, etc.). | The IRS usually allows you to deduct **50 %** of the cost of business meals.  | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Receipts for phone calls (if the expense is listed)** and email or fax charges that are used for business while traveling. | They can be deducted as a travel expense if they are necessary for the trip. | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Receipts for tips** (e.g., for hotel staff or transportation carriers). | Tips you give for business travel services are deductible. | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **A calendar or itineraries** that show the scheduling of your trip and the business reasons for each location visited. | Helps prove the trip is “ordinary and necessary” for your business. | (irs_publication
